current_state_summary:
As of July 2026 the observed global mean surface temperature (ERA5, vs 1850-1900) stands at 1.60 C for 2024 (first calendar year above 1.5 C), 1.47 C for 2025 (third warmest, 0.01 C below 2023's 1.48 C), and 1.47 +/- 0.08 C for January-June 2026 (third-warmest first half, behind 2024 and 2025). June 2026 was the second-warmest June globally at 1.39 C (16.54 C absolute) but Western Europe's warmest June on record (20.74 C, +3.06 C vs 1991-2020); France set its hottest national day on record on 24 June (national mean 30.0 C, peak 43.8 C). Berkeley Earth's June update gives 2026 roughly a 12% chance of being the warmest year and ~72% odds the annual mean exceeds 1.5 C. The 2023-2024 step-change did not persist as a further ratchet: 2025 and 2026 to date sit slightly below the 2024 peak, consistent with ENSO discharge plus a persistent underlying trend of ~0.024-0.030 C/yr. Hansen reports Earth's energy imbalance at 1.58 W/m2 over Jan 2025-Mar 2026 and attributes much of the recent surge to record-low planetary albedo (aerosol/shipping-fuel cleanup), a view still contested against the IPCC framing.

ENSO has flipped hard. Niño 3.4 reached +2.1 C in the week centred on 15 July 2026; 23 of 26 models in the mid-July ensemble project a very strong (>= +2.0 C) event peaking OND 2026, with a ~97% chance El Niño persists into early 2027. NOAA cut the Atlantic hurricane outlook to 55% below-normal, 8-14 named storms; CSU's 8 July update forecasts 9 named storms and 1 major hurricane. This loads a very high probability of a record-warm 2027 and of large El Niño-driven fire/flood/drought anomalies in Indonesia, Amazonia, East Africa and Australia.

Carbon: Mauna Loa hit 432 ppm in May 2026; the Met Office forecasts a 2026 annual mean of 429.4 +/- 0.6 ppm, +2.37 ppm on 2025. Decadal growth in the 2020s is 2.63 ppm/yr versus 2.41 in the 2010s; 2024's +3.75 ppm was the largest one-year rise on record. Global Carbon Budget 2025 put fossil+cement CO2 at a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.1%). The IGCC 4th edition puts human-induced warming at 1.37 C in 2025 and the remaining 1.5 C budget at 130 GtCO2 at 1 Jan 2026 - about three years of emissions.

Cryosphere and ocean: Arctic sea ice set a record-low winter maximum on 15 March 2026 (14.28-14.29 Mkm2, second consecutive record low); the September 2025 minimum was 4.60 Mkm2, only tenth lowest. Antarctic sea ice rebounded to a near-average 2.58 Mkm2 minimum on 26 Feb 2026 (16th lowest), after four record/near-record years. Ocean heat content (0-2000 m) set a ninth consecutive record in 2025 with +23 ZJ, the largest annual gain since 2017. GMSL is rising ~4.5 mm/yr with acceleration ~0.84 mm/yr/decade. AMOC at 26 N averages ~16.9 Sv with a RAPID-observed decline near 1 Sv/decade (some analyses 2.6 Sv/decade); 2026 papers (Portmann et al., Science Advances) constrain ~50% weakening by 2100, but no collapse signal is detected.

Losses: 2025 global economic nat-cat losses were USD 220 bn with USD 107 bn insured (sixth straight >100 bn year; 92% from secondary perils; LA wildfires alone USD 40 bn insured). H1 2026 insured losses were only USD 46 bn, 28% below the 10-year H1 average and the lowest since 2018, with five consecutive quarters lacking a single >10 bn event. IDMC's 2026 report: 29.9 M disaster displacements in 2025, exceeded for the first time by 32.3 M conflict displacements. COP31 convenes in Antalya 9-20 November 2026 under a Türkiye presidency with Australia leading negotiations.

indicators.label: Global mean surface temperature anomaly vs 1850-1900 (ERA5/C3S, annual)
indicators.source: Copernicus C3S / ERA5 monthly climate bulletins; 2025 annual = 1.47 C, 2024 = 1.60 C, Jan-Jun 2026 = 1.47 +/- 0.08 C. https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-bulletin

indicators.label: Atmospheric CO2, Mauna Loa annual mean
indicators.source: NOAA GML Mauna Loa trends + Met Office 2026 CO2 forecast (429.4 +/- 0.6 ppm annual mean, +2.37 ppm on 2025; May 2026 monthly 432 ppm). https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/

indicators.label: Niño 3.4 SST anomaly (weekly/ONI-equivalent)
indicators.source: NOAA CPC ENSO diagnostic discussion + IRI July 2026 Quick Look; weekly Niño 3.4 +2.1 C centred 15 Jul 2026, 23/26 models forecast >= +2.0 C peak in OND 2026. https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/enso/current/

indicators.label: Arctic sea ice September minimum extent
indicators.source: NSIDC Sea Ice Today; 2025 minimum 4.60 Mkm2 on 10 Sep, tenth lowest in 47-yr record; record low 3.39 Mkm2 (2012). https://nsidc.org/sea-ice-today/analyses

indicators.label: AMOC transport at 26N (RAPID array annual mean)
indicators.source: RAPID-MOCHA 26N array; recent mean ~16.9 Sv, observed decline ~1 Sv/decade over 2004-2025 (range 0.4-1.6; some analyses 2.6 +/- 0.7 Sv/decade). Portmann et al. 2026 Science Advances. https://climate.metoffice.cloud/amoc.html

indicators.label: Global natural catastrophe total economic losses (nominal)
indicators.source: Swiss Re sigma 1/2026: 2025 economic losses USD 220 bn, insured USD 107 bn (49% insured share, a record). 2024 was ~USD 320-328 bn. https://www.swissre.com/institute/research/sigma-research/sigma-2026-01-natcat-2025-wildfire-storm-risk.html

indicators.label: Global weather/climate extreme event frequency index (EM-DAT climate-related disaster count, 1991-2020 mean = 100)
indicators.source: EM-DAT / CRED annual disaster counts, normalised to the 1991-2020 mean (~330 events/yr); recent years running 350-400. Cross-checked against Gallagher Re billion-dollar event counts (H1 2026: 11 vs 10-yr H1 average 16).

indicators.label: Global fossil-fuel + cement CO2 emissions
indicators.source: Global Carbon Budget 2025 (ESSD 18, 3211, 2026): record 38.1 GtCO2, +1.1% on 2024; coal +1.0%, oil +1.1%, gas +1.3%; total CO2 incl. land use ~42 GtCO2 and roughly flat. https://globalcarbonbudget.org/

indicators.label: Remaining carbon budget for 50% chance of 1.5C
indicators.source: Indicators of Global Climate Change 4th edition (Forster et al., 2026): 130 GtCO2 at 1 Jan 2026, ~3 years at current emissions; ~110 GtCO2 by mid-2026 after ~21 GtCO2 of H1 emissions. https://climate.leeds.ac.uk/

indicators.label: Global mean sea level rise since January 1993 (satellite altimetry)
indicators.source: NASA/JPL + Copernicus sea level indicator; current rate ~4.5 mm/yr (vs 2.1 mm/yr in 1993), acceleration 0.84 mm/yr/decade over 2005-2023. https://climate.copernicus.eu/climate-indicators/sea-level

indicators.label: Upper-2000m ocean heat content anomaly vs 1981-2010 (IAP/NOAA blend)
indicators.source: Cheng et al., Advances in Atmospheric Sciences (Jan 2026): 2025 set a ninth consecutive OHC record with +23 ZJ, versus +16 ZJ in 2024; largest annual gain since 2017. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0

indicators.label: Antarctic sea ice February minimum extent
indicators.source: NSIDC: 2026 minimum 2.58 Mkm2 on 26 Feb, sixteenth lowest in 48-yr record, 0.73 Mkm2 above the 2023 record low and 0.26 Mkm2 below the 1981-2010 average - a rebound after four record/near-record years. https://nsidc.org/news-analyses/news-stories/antarctic-sea-ice-extent-arrives-near-average-minimum

indicators.label: Greenland Ice Sheet annual mass balance
indicators.source: PROMICE/DMI + GRACE-FO; hydrological year 2024-25 loss 139 +/- 79 Gt; 2002-2025 mean -264 Gt/yr; 2010s mean -242 +/- 17 Gt/yr. NOAA Arctic Report Card 2025.

indicators.label: Cumulative share of the original Amazon biome deforested
indicators.source: INPE PRODES / MapBiomas / RAISG; ~17-18% of the original biome cleared, with a further ~17% degraded. Brazilian Amazon clearing fell sharply 2023-2025 from the 2021-22 peak. Modelled critical range 20-25% deforestation combined with 1.5-2 C warming (PNAS 2025; Nature 2026).

indicators.label: Global wildfire carbon emissions (CAMS GFAS)
indicators.source: Copernicus CAMS Global Fire Assimilation System annual totals; record ~2170 MtC in 2023 (Canadian megafire year); typical range 1700-2100 MtC with strong El Nino-year peaks (1997 Indonesian peat fires, 2015-16).

events.statement: Sustained (multi-year) exceedance of 1.5 C: the 10-year running mean of global mean surface temperature reaches or exceeds 1.5 C above 1850-1900.
events.resolution_criteria: WMO's State of the Global Climate (or C3S/ERA5 equivalent) reports a completed 10-calendar-year mean GMST anomaly >= 1.500 C above 1850-1900 in the consolidated multi-dataset average. The decade 2016-2025 averaged 1.33 C (ERA5).
events.reference_class: Threshold crossing of a monotone trending series rather than a repeatable hazard. IPCC AR6 and post-AR6 assessments place the 20-yr-centred 1.5 C crossing in the early-to-mid 2030s; the observable 10-yr running mean crosses several years earlier. Reference class = spread of CMIP6/observationally-constrained crossing dates, roughly 2029-2040, i.e. ~11 candidate years.
events.reasoning: Arithmetic: ERA5 decadal mean 2016-2025 = (1.29+1.22+1.15+1.30+1.34+1.19+1.23+1.48+1.60+1.47)/10 = 1.327 C. It must rise 0.173 C. Rolling the window forward drops cool 2017-2018 (~1.18) and adds trend years at ~1.50-1.60, so the running mean gains ~0.035-0.045 C/yr. Extrapolating: window ending 2030 ~1.47, ending 2031 ~1.51. So the mechanical crossing lands ~2031-2033, with tail cases 2029 (if the super El Nino plus continued albedo forcing pushes 2027-2029 to 1.65-1.75) and 2036 (if aerosol/volcanic cooling intervenes). Hazard is near-zero now and ramps: base rate 0.09/yr over an 11-year candidate window, multiplied by 0.25 today because the mean is mechanically 0.17 C short and can move at most ~0.045 C/yr, giving ~0.023/yr for 2026-2027 -> p_by_2027 0.03. By 2030 the hazard is ~0.10/yr and by 2032 ~0.40/yr, giving p_by_2030 0.20 and p_by_2036 0.90. The residual 10% covers a large volcanic eruption, a strong multi-year La Nina regime, or a downward dataset revision.

events.statement: A single calendar year with global mean surface temperature >= 2.0 C above 1850-1900 in a major observational dataset.
events.resolution_criteria: Copernicus C3S/ERA5 or Berkeley Earth reports a completed calendar-year global anomaly >= 2.00 C above the 1850-1900 baseline. Current record: 2024 at 1.60 C (ERA5).
events.reference_class: Never observed in 176 years of record. Nearest analogue: single-year jumps above the prior record. The largest observed year-on-year record margin is 2023->2024 (+0.12 C) and 2015->2016 (+0.14 C). No year has ever exceeded the standing record by 0.40 C.
events.reasoning: Decompose: annual anomaly = trend + ENSO + noise. Trend level in 2026 is ~1.48 C rising 0.024 C/yr, so ~1.72 C in 2036 (0.030 C/yr Hansen-style acceleration gives ~1.82 C). A record super El Nino (Nino 3.4 already +2.1 C in July 2026, forecast peak >= +2.0 to +2.9 C in OND) adds ~+0.14-0.18 C to the following year, so 2027 projects to ~1.68-1.78 C - short of 2.0 by ~0.25 C, which is ~2.3 sigma on interannual vol of 0.11 C. Hence p(2027) ~ 0.015. By 2036 the trend-only gap is ~0.28 C (2.5 sigma) in the central case but only ~0.18 C (1.6 sigma) under accelerated warming, and El Nino years shift the mean +0.15. Weighting ~25% on the accelerated-trend branch and ~15% of years being strong El Ninos gives ~0.015-0.02/yr terminal hazard, ~0.13-0.15 cumulative. Consistency check: base 0.006 x 2.2 = 0.0132/yr; 1-(1-0.0132)^10.4 = 0.129, close to the stated 0.14 (slight uplift for trend growth over the window). Multiplier 2.2 is justified by the record El Nino, record-low planetary albedo (Earth energy imbalance 1.58 W/m2, Jan 2025-Mar 2026), and record OHC - not by 10x journalism.

events.statement: First ice-free Arctic day: Arctic sea ice extent falls below 1.0 million km2 on at least one day.
events.resolution_criteria: NSIDC Sea Ice Index daily total Arctic extent (5-day trailing mean) drops below 1.00 million km2 on any day, as confirmed in an NSIDC analysis post.
events.reference_class: Never observed in the 47-year satellite record. Lowest daily extent ever: 3.39 Mkm2 (Sep 2012); 2025 minimum 4.60 Mkm2 (tenth lowest). Kim et al. 2024 (Nat Comms) using 11 CMIP6 models / 366 members: median first ice-free day in the 2030s-2040s, earliest ensemble members 2027-2030, and early cases always occur inside a rapid-ice-loss event.
events.reasoning: The gap is enormous: 4.60 -> below 1.00 Mkm2 is a 3.6 Mkm2 drop, and even the 2012 record was 3.39. The September-minimum trend is roughly -0.05 Mkm2/yr with residual SD ~0.42, so the trend minimum in 2036 is ~4.1 Mkm2; reaching <1.0 requires a rapid-ice-loss event of the kind CMIP6 members only produce after the trend minimum falls near ~2.5-3.0 Mkm2. Base rate 0.012/yr is taken as the fraction of CMIP6 ensemble members recording a first ice-free day per year during the 2030s. Multiplier 1.5 reflects two consecutive record-low winter maxima (14.29 Mkm2 on 15 Mar 2026, 14.32 on 22 Mar 2025) implying thin, young ice - but tempered by 2025's minimum being only tenth lowest, which argues against imminent collapse. Hazard is strongly ramping (near zero to 2029), so p_by_2027 0.004 and p_by_2030 0.035 undershoot the naive constant-hazard reconciliation while p_by_2036 0.16 matches 1-(1-0.018)^10.4 = 0.17.

events.statement: Detection of AMOC collapse onset: sustained transport collapse or an authoritative declaration that shutdown is underway.
events.resolution_criteria: Either (a) the RAPID 26N annual-mean AMOC transport falls below 10.0 Sv in two consecutive calendar years, or (b) the IPCC, WMO, NOAA or a comparable national assessment body states in an official report that an AMOC collapse/shutdown is underway rather than projected.
events.reference_class: Zero AMOC collapses in the ~70-year instrumental era and ~11,700 years of the Holocene. Paleoclimate Dansgaard-Oeschger/Heinrich transitions recur every ~1-2 kyr but only under glacial boundary conditions (~0.0007/yr). Modern estimates: Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen 2023 central 2050 (range 2025-2095, heavily criticised for its statistical assumptions); van Westen et al. 2024 'on route to tipping'; most CMIP6 models show no collapse before 2100; Portmann et al. 2026 (Sci Adv) constrain ~50% weakening by 2100 - severe but not collapse.
events.reasoning: Criterion (a) is arithmetically remote: from 16.9 Sv, reaching a sustained sub-10 Sv state requires a 7 Sv drop, ~30-70 years at the observed 0.1-0.26 Sv/yr trend, or a genuine nonlinear transition. RAPID interannual SD is ~1.3 Sv (observed range 14.6-18 Sv), so two consecutive years below 10 is ~5 sigma of noise and effectively requires the physical tipping. Criterion (b) is the realistic path within a decade and depends on assessment-body language, which has shifted noticeably in 2026 (an EGUsphere opinion piece titled 'The AMOC is weakening - time to take the evidence seriously'; a four-site two-decade decline paper in April 2026) but is also actively contested by natural-variability analyses. Base rate 0.002/yr sits between the Holocene rate (~0) and the aggressive Ditlevsen hazard (~0.014/yr). Multiplier 2.5 for freshening, the 2026 literature shift and record Greenland/Arctic forcing gives 0.005/yr: 1-(0.995)^1.4 = 0.007, ^4.4 = 0.022, ^10.4 = 0.051. Confidence low because the resolution partly depends on institutional language, not physics.

events.statement: Amazon crosses a large-scale dieback threshold.
events.resolution_criteria: Both of: (i) peer-reviewed flux/inventory evidence that the Amazon basin as a whole has been a net annual carbon source for three or more consecutive years; and (ii) MapBiomas/INPE/RAISG confirm that at least 25% of the original biome has been converted to non-forest or structurally degraded savanna-like state. Alternatively, an IPCC assessment or the Science Panel for the Amazon formally states that the dieback tipping threshold has been crossed.
events.reference_class: No biome-scale dieback of a major tropical rainforest has been observed in the instrumental record (0 events in ~120 years). The basin has flipped to a net carbon source only transiently, during the 2005, 2010, 2015-16 and 2023-24 droughts. Threshold literature: Nobre/Lovejoy 20-25% deforestation; PNAS 2025 gives near-system-wide transition of 62-77% of area at 1.5-1.9 C warming combined with 22-28% deforestation; current deforestation ~17-18%.
events.reasoning: Deforestation is at ~17.6% and rising ~0.09 pct/yr after the sharp 2023-2025 Brazilian slowdown; on that path 25% is not reached before ~2100, so criterion (ii) requires a policy reversal plus fire-driven degradation. Criterion (i) requires three consecutive net-source years, which needs back-to-back droughts - plausible in a 2026-27 super El Nino followed by continued warming, but the basin recovered to sink status after every previous drought. Base rate 0.004/yr encodes 'no observed instance in ~120 years, but the reference class is thin and models place non-trivial probability this century'. Multiplier 2.5 for the record 2023-24 drought, the loss of resilience documented since the 2000s in ~75% of the forest, and an incoming super El Nino - offset partly by falling Brazilian clearing rates. 0.010/yr gives 1-(0.99)^1.4 = 0.014, ^4.4 = 0.043, ^10.4 = 0.099. Confidence low: this event is dominated by definitional choices as much as by physical dynamics.

events.statement: Global natural-catastrophe economic losses in a single calendar year reach USD 500 billion (nominal, year-of-occurrence dollars).
events.resolution_criteria: Swiss Re sigma or Munich Re NatCatSERVICE reports total global economic losses from natural catastrophes >= USD 500 bn for a single calendar year, in nominal dollars as first published. 2025 = USD 220 bn; 2024 = ~USD 320-328 bn; nominal record ~USD 355 bn (2011).
events.reference_class: Years with global nat-cat economic losses at or above 2x the trailing-decade mean, 1980-2025: 1995 (Kobe), 2005 (Katrina/Rita/Wilma), 2011 (Tohoku + Thai floods) and marginally 2017 (Harvey/Irma/Maria) - 3-4 in 46 years, or 0.065-0.087/yr. The USD 500 bn nominal bar is currently ~2.0x the trailing-decade mean of ~USD 250 bn.
events.reasoning: This is an eroding bar, so the hazard rises mechanically. Nominal loss trend grows ~5-6%/yr (exposure growth plus inflation), so the trailing mean of ~USD 250 bn today becomes ~USD 420 bn by 2036 - at which point USD 500 bn is only ~1.2x the mean rather than 2.0x. Multiplier 0.55 applies to 2026-27 specifically: the bar is at its hardest relative to current means, H1 2026 insured losses were only USD 46 bn (28% below the 10-yr H1 average, lowest since 2018, five straight quarters with no >USD 10 bn event), and the strong El Nino is suppressing Atlantic hurricanes (NOAA 55% below-normal; CSU 8 July cut to 9 named storms, 1 major). That gives ~0.036/yr now: p_by_2027 = 1-(0.964)^1.4 = 0.049, reduced to 0.035 because the 2026 season is already half-elapsed and benign. Average hazard ~0.05/yr to 2030 gives 0.20, and ~0.08/yr average to 2036 gives 1-(0.92)^10.4 = 0.58. The realistic paths are a major-metropolitan US landfalling hurricane (Miami/Houston/NYC), a Tokyo or Nankai Trough earthquake, or a stacked La Nina-year US convective/hurricane season - not gradual accumulation.

events.statement: A single climate or weather hazard displaces at least 15 million people within a 12-month window.
events.resolution_criteria: IDMC's Global Report on Internal Displacement (or an equivalent UN/IOM tally) records at least 15 million displacements attributable to a single named hazard event or a single continuous hazard episode within 12 months. Historical maximum: China floods 2010, 15.2 million displacements.
events.reference_class: IDMC disaster-displacement records 2008-2025 (18 years): only China's 2010 floods reached ~15 million displacements from a single episode. Pakistan 2010 (~11 M) and Pakistan 2022 (8.2 M) are the next largest. So 1 clear instance in 18 years = 0.055/yr, with 2-3 near-misses.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.055/yr from 1 qualifying event in 18 years of IDMC record. Multiplier 1.9 combines: (i) a forecast record-strength El Nino peaking OND 2026, and the two largest South/East Asian flood-displacement years (2010, 2016) both followed strong ENSO extremes; (ii) continued exposure growth in South and Southeast Asian floodplains; (iii) precautionary pre-emptive evacuation becoming standard practice, which mechanically inflates IDMC displacement counts (Bangladesh, Philippines and India now routinely evacuate millions). Offsetting: China's post-2010 flood-control investment materially reduces the single largest historical contributor, which is why the multiplier is <2 rather than 3. Annual hazard 0.105 gives 1-(0.895)^1.4 = 0.14, ^4.4 = 0.39, ^10.4 = 0.68 - matching the stated 0.13/0.37/0.67 within rounding. Note IDMC's 2026 report recorded 29.9 M disaster displacements in 2025 in aggregate (13% above the decadal average) but no single event above ~5 M.

events.statement: A new record warmest calendar year is set, exceeding 2024's 1.60 C (ERA5) global anomaly.
events.resolution_criteria: Copernicus C3S reports a calendar year from 2026 onward as the warmest in the ERA5 record, with an anomaly above 1.60 C relative to 1850-1900. Attributed to the year itself, not the announcement date.
events.reference_class: New global annual temperature records, 1980-2025: 1981, 1983, 1987, 1988, 1990, 1995, 1997, 1998, 2005, 2010, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2023, 2024 - roughly 12-15 in 46 years, ~0.28/yr. More specifically: every strong-to-very-strong El Nino (1982-83, 1997-98, 2015-16, 2023-24) produced a record annual mean in the year of or immediately following the ENSO peak - 4 for 4.
events.reasoning: 2026 itself: Berkeley Earth's June update gives ~12% odds of a record and ~72% odds of exceeding 1.5 C, since the El Nino peaks too late in the year - call it 0.15. 2027: the ENSO-to-GMST lag is 3-5 months, so a Nino 3.4 peak of +2.0 to +2.9 C in OND 2026 loads the first half of 2027. Analogue arithmetic: 2015 (1.15) -> 2016 (1.29) was +0.14 after an ONI peak of +2.6; 2023 (1.48) -> 2024 (1.60) was +0.12 after +2.0. Applying the same to a 2026 base of ~1.50-1.53 gives 2027 around 1.64-1.70, comfortably above 1.60. Discounting for the possibility the El Nino underperforms the forecast or a volcanic eruption intervenes: p(2027 record) ~ 0.72. Combined: 1-(1-0.15)(1-0.72) = 0.76. Beyond 2027, the underlying 0.024 C/yr trend guarantees the 1.60 C mark is exceeded within a decade absent a major eruption, hence 0.98 by 2036. Hazard multiplier 2.6 x base 0.28 = 0.73/yr for the immediate window, at the ceiling of what current conditions justify.

events.statement: A volcanic eruption injects >= 5 Tg of SO2 into the stratosphere, producing >= 0.2 C of global cooling in the following 24 months.
events.resolution_criteria: OMPS/MLS or equivalent satellite retrievals confirm stratospheric SO2 loading >= 5 Tg from a single eruption, and NASA GISS or C3S subsequently attribute >= 0.2 C of global surface cooling to it.
events.reference_class: Eruptions with >= 5 Tg stratospheric SO2 since 1880: Krakatau 1883, Santa Maria 1902, Novarupta 1912, Agung 1963, El Chichon 1982, Pinatubo 1991 - 6 in ~145 years = 0.041/yr. Restricting to the satellite era (1979-2025): El Chichon and Pinatubo, 2 in 47 years = 0.043/yr. Hunga Tonga 2022 injected water vapour but only ~0.4-0.5 Tg SO2 and did not qualify.
events.reasoning: Volcanism is exogenous to climate forcing, so hazard_multiplier_now is exactly 1.0 - no current-conditions adjustment is defensible. Base rate 0.038/yr is the mean of the 1880-2025 and satellite-era counts. Reconciliation: 1-(0.962)^1.4 = 0.052, ^4.4 = 0.155, ^10.4 = 0.332. Exactly matches. Included because it is the single largest downside shock to every warming-threshold event in this domain: a Pinatubo-class eruption in, say, 2029 would delay the sustained-1.5 C crossing by 2-3 years and cut the single-year-above-2 C probability by roughly half. Impact size of -2.2 SD on gmst_anomaly_c reflects Pinatubo's -0.25 C peak against an interannual vol of 0.11 C.

events.statement: Global wildfire carbon emissions in a single calendar year exceed 2400 MtC.
events.resolution_criteria: Copernicus CAMS Global Fire Assimilation System reports annual global wildfire carbon emissions above 2400 MtC for a calendar year. Standing record ~2170 MtC (2023).
events.reference_class: Years setting a new global fire-emissions record in the GFAS/GFED era (2003-2025): roughly 3-4 in 23 years, ~0.15/yr for any record, but only ~0.05/yr for a record exceeding the prior mark by >10%. The two largest global fire-emission anomalies attributable to a single region (1997 and 2015 Indonesian peat fires, ~0.8-2.6 GtC and ~0.6 GtC respectively) both occurred in very strong El Nino years - 2 for 2.
events.reasoning: Current level 1900 MtC with vol 230; 2400 is 2.2 sigma. But the ENSO coupling shifts the distribution: an elasticity of ~1.1 SD of wildfire emissions per SD of Nino 3.4, at a forecast +2.5 C peak (~2.8 SD of the ENSO series), moves the conditional mean to roughly 2300-2500 MtC for the Indonesian/Amazonian fire seasons of late 2026 and 2027. That makes 2400 roughly a coin-flip-to-one-in-three per El Nino year. Multiplier 3.0 is at the doctrinal ceiling and is justified specifically by 2-for-2 historical analogues plus 115,000 ha already burned in France (a national record) and 320,000+ evacuated in Spain and France by 27 July 2026. p_by_2027 0.24 (fire seasons of Aug-Nov 2026 and 2027); after the El Nino decays the hazard falls back toward 0.04/yr, giving only +0.14 over 2028-2030 and +0.22 over 2031-2036. Reconciliation is deliberately front-loaded rather than constant-hazard.

events.statement: A single heatwave episode is attributed with >= 50,000 excess deaths within a 60-day window.
events.resolution_criteria: A peer-reviewed epidemiological attribution study (e.g. Nature Medicine / Lancet Planetary Health / EuroMOMO-based analyses) estimates >= 50,000 heat-attributable excess deaths from a single heatwave episode spanning no more than 60 days, in one or more countries.
events.reference_class: Episodes meeting this bar since 2000: European heatwave 2003 (~70,000), Russian heatwave 2010 (~55,000), and the summer 2022 European heat season (~62,000 EU-wide, though spread over more than 60 days). That is 2-3 in 26 years = 0.077-0.115/yr, with 2015 India/Pakistan, 2023 Europe (~47,000) and 2025 Europe as near-misses.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.11/yr from 2-3 qualifying episodes in 26 years. Multiplier 1.7 for: Europe warming at roughly twice the global rate; June 2026 already Western Europe's warmest June on record at +3.06 C vs 1991-2020 with France's hottest-ever day (national mean 30.0 C, 43.8 C peak) on 24 June; WHO citing >200,000 European heat deaths over the past four years; and rising exposure of elderly populations in Europe, East Asia and the Gulf. The multiplier is held well below 3 because adaptation (air conditioning penetration, heat-health early warning systems) is demonstrably reducing heat mortality per degree in Europe, and because the 2003 and 2010 events were partly artefacts of unprepared populations. Annual hazard 0.187: 1-(0.813)^1.4 = 0.25 - I raise p_by_2027 to 0.31 because the ongoing summer 2026 Northern Hemisphere heat season is already extreme and may resolve this. p_by_2030 = 1-(0.813)^4.4 = 0.58 (stated 0.60), p_by_2036 = 1-(0.813)^10.4 = 0.88. Resolution typically lags the event by 9-18 months as attribution studies are published.

events.statement: A state or state-backed programme conducts or formally commits to operational stratospheric aerosol injection at >= 1,000 tonnes/year scale.
events.resolution_criteria: A national government, coalition of governments, or state-funded entity publicly announces an operational (not research) SAI deployment programme with a stated injection rate of at least 1,000 t/yr of sulphate or equivalent aerosol precursor, or independent monitoring confirms such injection is occurring.
events.reference_class: Zero instances ever. Nearest analogues: commercial micro-efforts at the tonnes scale (Make Sunsets, since 2022) and one aborted UK outdoor experiment (SPICE, 2011). The regulatory tide has run the other way - Mexico banned solar geoengineering experiments in 2023 and several US states legislated bans in 2024-2025, while the 2024 UNEA non-use resolution stalled.
events.reasoning: No reference class exists, so the base rate is constructed as 'novel state technology deployment with a decade-scale credible pathway and active political opposition', which historically resolves at low single-digit percent per year. Multiplier 2.0 for: the 1.5 C budget effectively exhausted (130 GtCO2 at 1 Jan 2026, ~3 years), record-low albedo already demonstrating the leverage of aerosol forcing, and rising research funding in the US, UK (ARIA) and China. Held to 2.0, not higher, because the binding constraint is political and legal rather than technical, and 2023-2025 policy moved decisively toward restriction. Annual hazard 0.008: 1-(0.992)^1.4 = 0.011, ^4.4 = 0.035, ^10.4 = 0.080. Included because it is the highest-leverage cross-domain coupling in the climate block: deployment would decouple gmst_anomaly_c from co2_ppm and invalidate most threshold events above.

couplings.mechanism: El Nino discharges tropical Pacific ocean heat to the atmosphere and reduces low-cloud cover; observed GMST response is ~0.07-0.10 C per 1 C of Nino 3.4 anomaly, peaking 3-5 months after the ENSO peak. 1 SD of Nino 3.4 (0.9 C) therefore moves GMST ~0.07 C, or ~0.6 SD of its 0.11 C interannual vol.

El Nino suppresses the tropical land carbon sink through drought and raises fire emissions, boosting the CO2 growth rate by 0.5-1.0 ppm/yr. 2015-16 (+3.0 ppm) and 2023-24 (+3.75 ppm) both followed strong El Ninos. 1 SD of Nino 3.4 lifts the growth rate ~0.5 ppm against a 0.7 ppm SD.

El Nino dries Indonesian peatlands, Amazonia and Australia simultaneously. The 1997-98 and 2015-16 events produced the two largest single-region fire-emission anomalies on record. The response is strongly convex in ENSO amplitude, so this elasticity is a lower bound for very strong events.

El Nino raises Atlantic vertical wind shear and suppresses hurricane activity, which is the single largest driver of global insured losses; the flood/drought losses it generates in Asia, East Africa and Latin America are less insured and smaller in dollar terms. Net effect on the global economic-loss total is modestly negative in the short run.

Radiative forcing from CO2 (5.35*ln(C/C0) W/m2) with a transient climate response of ~1.8 C per doubling. Slow relative to the ENSO channel; the elasticity is small on annual timescales because 1 SD of CO2 growth variability is only 0.7 ppm.

Roughly 44-48% of emitted CO2 stays airborne within the year; 1 GtCO2 emitted raises concentration ~0.128 ppm before sink uptake, so emission-rate variability maps near one-for-one onto growth-rate variability.

Definitional: the budget depletes by total annual CO2 emissions (~42 GtCO2/yr including land use). The elasticity is below 1.0 only because periodic methodological revisions to the budget (TCRE, non-CO2 forcing assumptions) inject independent variance.

Roughly 3 million km2 of September ice lost per 1 C of global warming (observed 1979-2025), but on annual timescales summer melt is dominated by spring atmospheric circulation and Arctic Dipole patterns rather than global mean temperature, so the year-to-year elasticity is modest.

Southern Ocean subsurface warming has raised the probability of low-extent years since 2016, but Antarctic sea ice is dominated by wind-driven variability (the 2026 rebound to 2.58 Mkm2 was caused by strong southerly winds in the Weddell Sea), so the thermal coupling is weak.

Clausius-Clapeyron scaling of ~7% more atmospheric moisture per degree, plus a strongly nonlinear increase in heat-extreme exceedance frequency. Contemporaneous; the reported index also carries substantial non-climatic reporting-bias variance, which caps the elasticity.

Co-variation under a common Earth energy imbalance forcing (1.58 W/m2 over Jan 2025-Mar 2026); ~90% of excess heat enters the ocean. Causality partly runs the other way on interannual timescales, since El Nino years transfer ocean heat to the atmosphere and briefly slow OHC growth.
Thermosteric expansion contributes ~1.3-1.5 mm/yr of the ~4.5 mm/yr total; the rest is land-ice mass loss and terrestrial water storage, which are the dominant sources of interannual GMSL variance.
360 Gt of ice loss equals 1 mm of sea level rise. More negative mass balance raises GMSL, hence the negative sign. Greenland contributes ~0.7-0.8 mm/yr of the current total.

Greenland meltwater freshens the subpolar North Atlantic and suppresses deep convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas. Sign is positive because a less negative mass balance means less freshwater and a stronger AMOC. The coupling is weak on decadal timescales - a 2026 eddying-model study found only a weak 21st-century AMOC response to Greenland meltwater.

A weaker AMOC reduces northward heat transport, cooling the North Atlantic and Northern Hemisphere land while allowing slight Southern Hemisphere warming; the net global effect is small and slow, and mostly a redistribution rather than a change in the energy budget.

Losses are driven by the joint distribution of event count and exposure at the point of impact; a heavy tail means a single landfall over a major metro dominates any given year, which is why the elasticity to event count alone is only moderate. In 2025 secondary perils drove a record 92% of the USD 107 bn insured total.

Fire carbon emissions add to the atmospheric burden, but most savanna and boreal fire carbon is reabsorbed by regrowth within a few years. Only peat and old-growth deforestation fire emissions are effectively permanent, which is why the elasticity is well below the fossil-emissions channel.

Cleared and fragmented forest edges dry out and become ignition-prone; deforestation-driven drying lowers the Amazon's climate threshold (Nature 2026), so clearing raises fire emissions with a lag through edge effects rather than instantaneously.

Cross-domain (economics/finance). Reinsurance renewal pricing responds to prior-year loss experience with roughly a 9-month lag; the five-quarter benign streak through H1 2026 (USD 46 bn insured, lowest H1 since 2018) is already driving soft-market conditions and price reductions.

Cross-domain (agriculture/commodities). Simultaneous heat and drought in multiple breadbaskets raises grain prices; a strong El Nino specifically threatens Southeast Asian rice, Australian wheat and Southern African maize while often benefiting Argentine and US harvests, which damps the net elasticity.

Cross-domain (governance). Record temperature years and salient disasters raise policy salience with a lag of roughly 18 months through electoral and COP cycles, but the 2024-2026 period demonstrates that political backlash and energy-security priorities can decouple policy from physical signals entirely.

key_uncertainties: Whether the post-2023 warming acceleration is a permanent forcing change (aerosol/shipping-fuel cleanup driving record-low planetary albedo, per Hansen's 1.58 W/m2 energy imbalance) or a transient ENSO-plus-Hunga excursion. This single question moves annual_drift on gmst_anomaly_c between 0.020 and 0.035 C/yr and roughly triples the probability of single_year_above_2c by 2036.

The magnitude of the 2026-27 El Nino. Models project a peak Nino 3.4 of +2.0 to +2.9 C, but the July value of +2.1 C is already unprecedentedly early and high, and ENSO forecasts routinely bust between July and the following winter. A bust would remove roughly 0.15 C from the 2027 anomaly and cut new_record_warm_year from 0.76 to ~0.45.

AMOC observational adequacy: RAPID's 22-year record is short relative to multidecadal variability, and 2026 produced both papers arguing for a sustained basin-wide weakening since 1960 and counter-analyses attributing most of the signal to natural variability. Neither the amoc_strength drift (-0.11 vs -0.26 Sv/yr) nor the amoc_collapse_signal hazard can be pinned down from observations alone.

Definition dependence of the tipping-element events. Both amazon_dieback_threshold and amoc_collapse_signal resolve substantially on institutional language rather than a crisp physical measurement, which is why both are marked low confidence.

Whether the benign 2025-2026 catastrophe-loss period reflects genuine ENSO-driven suppression of the Atlantic hurricane peril or short-run luck. Five consecutive quarters without a >USD 10 bn event is an unusual run given the underlying exposure trend, and reversion could be abrupt.

Data continuity risk. NSIDC had to rely on a Japanese satellite for the 2025 September minimum call after US satellite data problems, and IDMC reported reduced displacement-data availability in 15% of monitored countries in 2025 (three times the 2024 share). Several of these indicators may degrade in quality over the simulation window.

Arctic sea ice has not tracked the record-low winter maxima into record-low summer minima (2025 minimum was only tenth lowest despite two consecutive record-low maxima), which suggests the winter and summer systems are less tightly coupled than a simple thickness argument implies.
Antarctic sea ice: whether the 2016-2025 low-extent regime represents a forced shift or decadal variability is unresolved, and the 2026 rebound to a near-average minimum is evidence for the latter.

Non-CO2 forcing: methane growth rates, aerosol trajectories in China and India, and any future stratospheric aerosol intervention could each shift the near-term temperature path by more than the CO2 uncertainty does.

Loss data are nominal and unadjusted for exposure growth. Any simulation using annual_disaster_losses_bn must handle the fact that the USD 500 bn threshold erodes roughly 5-6% per year in real terms, making single_year_disaster_loss_500bn a rising-hazard event by construction.
surprises_2026: A very strong, potentially record El Nino developed far faster than mid-2025 forecasts implied: weekly Nino 3.4 reached +2.1 C by 15 July 2026, and 23 of 26 models in the mid-July ensemble project a very strong (>= +2.0 C) peak in Oct-Dec 2026, with ~97% odds of persistence into early spring 2027. A July value of +2.1 C exceeds the July readings of both 1997 (~+1.7) and 2015 (~+1.3).

Arctic sea ice set a record-low winter maximum for the second consecutive year: 14.28-14.29 million km2 on 15 March 2026 (NASA/NSIDC), about 29,000 km2 below the March 2025 record; the Met Office recorded the lowest March monthly mean at 14.17 Mkm2.

Antarctic sea ice reversed course: the 26 February 2026 minimum of 2.58 million km2 was only sixteenth lowest in 48 years and 730,000 km2 above the 2023 record low - a near-average minimum after four consecutive record or near-record low years, driven by strong southerly winds in the Weddell Sea.

Catastrophe losses were unusually low. Gallagher Re put H1 2026 insured nat-cat losses at USD 46 bn, 28% below the 10-year H1 average and the lowest H1 since 2018 (versus USD 84 bn in H1 2025), with only 11 billion-dollar events versus a 16-event average, and five consecutive quarters without a single >USD 10 bn event - the first H1 since 2020 with no weather event above USD 5 bn.

Western Europe had its warmest June on record (20.74 C, +3.06 C vs 1991-2020) while the globe had only its second-warmest June (1.39 C, 16.54 C absolute). France recorded its hottest day ever on 24 June 2026 with a national mean of 30.0 C and 43.8 C at Pulluau.

A severe Iberian/French wildfire outbreak in July 2026: by 27 July, fires had killed at least 16 civilians and three firefighters and forced more than 320,000 people from their homes in Spain and France alone, with France passing 115,000 hectares burned - a national record.

The 2023-24 warming step did not ratchet further. January-June 2026 averaged 1.47 +/- 0.08 C, the third-warmest first half behind 2024 and 2025, and 2025 finished at 1.47 C in ERA5 - third warmest, 0.01 C below 2023 and 0.13 C below 2024. Two datasets ranked 2025 second and six ranked it third.

The remaining 1.5 C carbon budget was cut to 130 GtCO2 as of 1 January 2026 in the fourth Indicators of Global Climate Change report (over 70 researchers, 56 institutions, 17 nations), roughly three years of emissions, with human-induced warming assessed at 1.37 C for 2025 and 1.5 C breach projected around 2030.

Ocean heat content set a ninth consecutive annual record in 2025 with an increase of 23 zettajoules in the upper 2000 m - the largest single-year gain since 2017 and up sharply from 16 ZJ in 2024 (Cheng et al., Advances in Atmospheric Sciences, January 2026).

Hurricane forecasts were slashed mid-season. NOAA's 2026 outlook gave a 55% chance of a below-normal Atlantic season with 8-14 named storms, and CSU's 8 July update cut to just 9 named storms and 1 major hurricane, potentially the least active season in over a decade.

AMOC literature shifted materially in 2026: Portmann et al. in Science Advances used observational constraints to project ~50% weakening by 2100, well above the CMIP6 multi-model mean; an April 2026 study documented two-decade decline across four independent deep-ocean monitoring sites; and an EGUsphere opinion paper argued the weakening evidence should now be taken seriously - alongside contrarian analyses emphasising natural variability.

IDMC's 2026 Global Report found that conflict and violence drove a record 32.3 million internal displacements in 2025, exceeding disaster displacements (29.9 million) for the first time on record, with 82.2 million people living in internal displacement across 104 countries.

Hansen's June 2026 analysis reported Earth's energy imbalance at 1.58 W/m2 for January 2025 - March 2026 and argued the planetary darkening since ~2013 is equivalent to more than 100 ppm of additional CO2, explicitly rejecting the framing that the 2026 heat is 'just the El Nino'.

The Met Office's 2026 Mauna Loa forecast is 429.4 +/- 0.6 ppm annual mean (+2.37 ppm on 2025), and May 2026 hit a monthly record of 432 ppm; the 2020s are running at 2.63 ppm/yr versus 2.41 ppm/yr in the 2010s, with 2024's +3.75 ppm the largest single-year rise ever measured.

Global Carbon Budget 2025 (published in ESSD in 2026) reported record fossil-fuel and cement CO2 emissions of 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.1%), with coal, oil and gas all above 2024 levels, while total CO2 including land use was roughly flat because land-use emissions fell and the land sink recovered.
